Content covers: the closing teaching that Temple functionaries' own sustenance comes from Heaven, illustrated by the fixed timing of kingdoms' own rise and fall (Belshazzar's night-fall, Egypt's day-fall); Hugras ben Levi's own unique vocal trill technique for the Levitical choir, using his own thumb and a finger between his lips; the mishnah's own further family remembered for shame, ben Kamtzar, for refusing to teach his own four-quill simultaneous-writing technique; the extended discussion of 'the name of the wicked shall rot,' including the story of Doeg ben Yosef weighed daily in gold by his own mother before being slaughtered, contrasted with naming children after the righteous (Zechariah) rather than the wicked (Doeg); Rabbi Elazar's own mirror-principle teachings that a righteous person is remembered by his own deeds while a wicked person is remembered only through another's; the Torah-source derivations for both 'the remembrance of the righteous is for a blessing' (from Abraham) and 'the name of the wicked shall rot' (from Sodom); the paired examples of Ovadia (righteous among the wicked Ahab and Jezebel) and Esav (wicked among the righteous); Rabbi Elazar's own further teachings on the mirror-principle between the blessings of the righteous and curses of the wicked, the world's own creation for the sake of a single righteous person, and the world's own continued endurance and generational renewal of the righteous through 'the feet of His pious ones'; the teaching that repeated resistance to sin brings divine protection from further sin; and the closing teaching on the self-reinforcing pull of both impurity and purity, illustrated by Rabbi Yishmael's own school's parable of a naphtha and balsam seller, closing into the daf-boundary comment that continues onto 39a.
